## Adding more sample metadata

***

We can use a joining function (`left_join()`) to combine the sample metadata in the `sample_meta` slot with our `samples_metadata` data frame from the [Data Import]() section of the case study. This adds columns such as Sex and Age to the sample metadata stored in the `spatialGE` object.

```{r}
scz_spatial@sample_meta <- scz_spatial@sample_meta %>% 
    dplyr::left_join(samples_metadata, by = c("sample_name" = "DxID"))
```

## Adding back a `spatial_meta` column name

***

We will pipe the `spatial_meta` data frame for each sample to an inline function (because of the curly braces) that finds the names of data frame (`names(.)`), evaluates which name(s) are equal to `NA` (`is.na()`) and uses the TRUEs and FALSEs that this returns to specify which name needs to be renamed with the specified name (`<- "cell_area"`). Finally the semicolon followed by a period (`; .`) is used to tag on another command, in this case to return the data frame after the name has been changed.

```{r}
for (sample_name in names(scz_spatial@spatial_meta)){
    scz_spatial@spatial_meta[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@spatial_meta[[sample_name]] %>%
        { names(.)[is.na(names(.))] <- "cell_area"; . }
}
```

## Filtering

***

### Using Control Probes and Codewords

First we create a function that we can use with `lapply` that takes the filtering thresholds that we found previously as well as each counts matrix as inputs. Notice that the thresholds are named arguments meaning they have default values set to the exact variables we were working with earlier. We don't have to specify them when we call the function because they have these default values. We find the combined expression within each cell of each of the three associated controls using column sums and identify the cell IDs where the combined expression of any one of these types of controls is greater than or equal to the 99th percentile threshold. Finally, we take a union of the identified cell IDs.

By calling this function with `lapply`, we'll have a named list (`to_remove_all`) where each sample name stores a vector of cell IDs that should be removed for that sample.

We use a `for` loop to then loop through the sample names and actually filter the cell IDs within the count matrix. Recall that the cells correspond to the columns in the count matrix. Our filter is specifically using an exclamation point (`!`) to specify that if a column name is **not** the list of cell IDs to be filtered, then keep it.

We use a `for` loop for the actual filtering because we don't want to output a list. Rather we want to overwite the `counts` slot, doing the same filtering steps for all of the samples (just using a different set of cell IDs to keep).

```{r}
findOverlap <- function(mat, negcp = negcontrol_probe_cutoff, negcc = negcontrol_cdwd_cutoff, ucc = unassigned_cdwd_cutoff){
    which_negcp <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlProbe"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcp))
    which_negcc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlCodeword"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcc))
    which_ucc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "Unassigned"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= ucc))

    to_remove <- union(union(which_negcp, which_negcc), which_ucc)

    return(to_remove)
}

to_remove_all <- lapply(scz_spatial@counts, findOverlap)

for (sample_name in names(to_remove_all)){
    scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]][,!colnames(scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]]) %in% to_remove_all[[sample_name]]]
}
```

How many cells do we have per sample now?

```{r}
lapply(scz_spatial@counts, ncol)
```

We also want to remove the spatial metadata information about these cells since they no longer have counts associated with them in the counts matrix. Recall that each row corresponds to a cell, and the cell IDs are stored in the `libname` column of the `spatial_meta` slot.

```{r}
for (sample_name in names(to_remove_all)){
    scz_spatial@spatial_meta[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@spatial_meta[[sample_name]][!scz_spatial@spatial_meta[[sample_name]]$libname %in% to_remove_all[[sample_name]],]
}
```

### Removing Control Probes and Codewords

Now that we've used the control probes and codewords to filter out cells, we can remove them as "genes" from our counts matrix.

```{r}
for (sample_name in names(scz_spatial@counts)){
    scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]][!grepl("^NegControl|Unassigned",rownames(scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]])), ]
}
```

All of the counts matrices will now be 300 rows representing data for the 300 Xenium panel genes.

```{r}
lapply(scz_spatial@counts, nrow)
```

### Using spatialGE

The filtering that we've done, while important, isn't enough. We also need to consider the overall library size of and number of features in cells. 

:::{.definition_box}
::::{.definition_box_header}
Library size and number of features
::::
::::{.inner_block}
The **library size** is the total sum of the counts in a single cell across genes. 

The **number of features** in a cell is the count of unique genes that have a count of at least one in a given cell.
::::
:::

Both the library size and the number of features in a cell serve as indicators of cell quality. Cells may be damaged during the sample extraction or preparation steps



```{r}
scz_spatial <- spatialGE::filter_data(scz_spatial,
                           spot_minreads=50,
                           spot_maxreads=3500,
                           spot_mingenes=10)
```

What do the summary statistics and distributions look like now?

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Table

```{r}
summarize_STlist(scz_spatial) %>% print(width = Inf)
```

Notice that the number of cells retained decreased for each sample again. Some decreased by only about one hundred while another sample decreased by a little over two thousand!

```{r}
distribution_plots(scz_spatial, plot_type='violin', plot_meta='total_counts')
```

## Normalizing

Transforming the raw mRNA counts is again necessary because of technical biases. Typically if working with single cell RNAseq data or data from sequencing based spatial transcriptomics assays (e.g., Visium), normalization methods try to correct for different sequencing depths in different cells. Typical methods used include log-transformation or the `SCTransform` method. The `spatialGE` package allows users to implement either of these with their spatially-resolved gene expression data. However, both of these methods are best suited to working with sequencing-based data rather than image-based data. @Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 and @Bhuva_etal_2024 discuss how these traditional methods may not be appropriate for spatial transcriptomics data, especialy data from image-based technologies. @Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 recommends using cell volume or cell area when available to normalize image-based data. @Bhuva_etal_2024 introduces a method `SpaNorm` which models library size effects while taking into account the spatial information inherent in the data. The `SpaNorm` method can't directly work with an `STlist` object from `spatialGE` without first converting it to a `SpatialExperiment` or `Seurat` object. Therefore, we won't perform normalization with `SpaNorm` within this case study. We will perform normalization with the typical methods and a cell area normalization.

Transformed counts are stored in the `tr_counts` slot and we can't store more than one set of transformed counts due to the "slot" nature of the data. Since we want to run more than one method and compare them, we will need multiple different `spatialGE` `STlist` objects. We'll duplicate two here, one that we can use with `SCTransform` and one we can use with a cell area normalization.

```{r}
scz_spatial_tr <- rlang::duplicate(scz_spatial)
scz_spatial_sct <- rlang::duplicate(scz_spatial)
```

### Log Transformation

Explain log transformation.

```{r}
scz_spatial <- spatialGE::transform_data(scz_spatial, method='log', cores=2)
```

When `spatialGE` performs normalization, besides adding data to the `tr_counts` slot for the transformed data, it [also does a couple of other tasks](https://github.com/FridleyLab/spatialGE/blob/849c174f2c1537dc871987dfefb68da91beb96e3/R/transform_data.R#L64-L113). First, it fills in the `gene_meta` slot. Previously this had been an empty list. Now it stores a data frame for each sample with the average and standard deviation expression for each gene. 

```{r}
names(scz_spatial@gene_meta)
head(scz_spatial@gene_meta[[1]])
```

Additionally, it stores information in the `misc` slot about the transformation approach that was used.

```{r}
scz_spatial@misc
```

### SCTransform

Explain SCTransform

```{r}
scz_spatial_sct <- transform_data(scz_spatial_sct, method = 'sct', cores = 2)
```

### Cell Area Normalization

@Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 recommends using cell volumes to normalize image-based data when it is available, but that cell area can be used instead. We do not have cell volumes, but we do have cell areas.

>We recommend, as first choice, cell volume normalization to account for such partial cell capture within imaged regions. Cell area may serve as a proxy where volume estimates are not available.

The `spatialGE` package does not currently support any additional normalization methods besides log-transformation and `SCTransform`. However, we can perform an alternate normalization method and store its results in our `STlist` object (`scz_spatial`), using data already present in `scz_spatial` because we brought over the `cell_area` column for each cell earlier in the [Data Import]() section of the case study. 

The cell area normalization procedure requires that:

* We find the median cell area for each sample
* Then find cell specific size factors by dividing each cell's area by the median. 
* We then scale the counts by these size factors.
* Finally, similarly to the log transformation method, we add a pseudocount of one so that there are no zeros before we use a logarithm to bring the values closer together.

This approach is used in the [OSTA book chapter for Xenium workflows](https://lmweber.org/OSTA/pages/img-workflow-xenium.html#processing) and adapts code from the [`scrapper` package](https://github.com/libscran/scrapper). 

Beyond performing and storing our cell area normalization, we'll also want to add the same further modifications to the `STlist` that `spatialGE` typically does. You might wonder -- if` those steps are not necessary for the normalization process, why are we doing them? We're going to do them because other functions from `spatialGE` may expect that information to be there. A strength of the `spatialGE` package and its web application is that later functions expect quality control and normalization steps were performed. So something that the transformation function does, we'll want to do so that later steps aren't expecting it and can't find it.

```{r}

run_area_transformation <- function(stlist_obj, sample){
    
    # find median cell area
    median_area <- median(stlist_obj@spatial_meta[[sample]]$cell_area)
    # calculate cell specific size factors based on cell area
    size_factors <- stlist_obj@spatial_meta[[sample]]$cell_area / median_area
    # transform the counts using these size factors
    norm <- t(t(stlist_obj@counts[[sample]])/size_factors)
    # add a pseudocount of one to the transformed values so there are not zeroes and use a logarithm base of 2 
    stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]] <- log1p(norm) / log(2)

    # find gene avgs and stdevs and store
    stlist_obj@gene_meta[[sample]] <- tibble::tibble(gene_mean=as.vector(Matrix::rowMeans(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]]))) %>%
      tibble::add_column(gene_stdevs=as.vector(apply(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]], 1, sd))) %>%
      add_column(gene=rownames(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]]), .before=1)

    return(stlist_obj)
}

for (sample_name in names(scz_spatial_tr@counts)){
    scz_spatial_tr <- run_area_transformation(scz_spatial_tr, sample_name)
}

scz_spatial_tr@misc[["transform"]] <- "cell_area"

```

### Visualize

We can visualize the library size for each cell within each sample.

```{r}
visualize_lib_size <- function(mat, title_name){
    Matrix::colSums(mat) %>% 
        as.data.frame() %>%
        ggplot(aes(x=`.`)) + geom_histogram(bins = 500) + theme_bw() + ggtitle(title_name)
}
```

This code creates a function that will accept a matrix and compute the sum down each column. The column sums are stored as a data frame and then visualized as a histogram.

We will call this function with `purrr::map2()` because this function allows us to loop through two inputs (`scz_spatial@counts` -- count matrices for each sample and `names(scz_spatial@counts)` -- a vector of sample names), returning 6 plots that we can combine using `patchwork::wrap_plots()` and add a title with `patchwork::plot_annotation()`.

:::{.panel-tabset}

#### Raw counts

```{r}
patchwork::wrap_plots(purrr::map2(scz_spatial@counts, names(scz_spatial@counts), visualize_lib_size), nrow = 2) + patchwork::plot_annotation(title = "Raw counts")
```

#### Log transformation

```{r}
wrap_plots(map2(scz_spatial@tr_counts, names(scz_spatial@tr_counts), visualize_lib_size), nrow = 2) + plot_annotation(title = "Log transformed counts")
```

#### SCTransform

```{r}
wrap_plots(map2(scz_spatial_sct@tr_counts, names(scz_spatial_sct@tr_counts), visualize_lib_size), nrow = 2) + plot_annotation(title = "SCTransform")
```

#### Cell area normalization

```{r}
wrap_plots(map2(scz_spatial_tr@tr_counts, names(scz_spatial_tr@tr_counts), visualize_lib_size), nrow = 2) + plot_annotation(title = "Cell area normalization")
```

:::

We can visualize the distribution of expression of a few genes (before and after the normalization) using the `distribution_plots()` function from `spatialGE`. If plotting multiple genes, this function returns a named list of the plots. We'll combine them using the `+` functionality from patchwork and using various patchwork functions to control the layout and annotation of the plots.

```{r}
raw_plots <- distribution_plots(scz_spatial, genes = c("CX3CR1", "FKBP5", "PVALB", "MBP"), data_type = "raw")

transformed_log_plots <- distribution_plots(scz_spatial, genes = c("CX3CR1", "FKBP5", "PVALB", "MBP"), data_type = "tr")

transformed_sct_plots <- distribution_plots(scz_spatial_sct, genes = c("CX3CR1", "FKBP5", "PVALB", "MBP"), data_type = "tr")

transformed_tr_plots <- distribution_plots(scz_spatial_tr, genes = c("CX3CR1", "FKBP5", "PVALB", "MBP"), data_type = "tr")
```

:::{.panel-tabset}

#### MBP

```{r}
raw_plots$MBP + ggtitle("Raw data") + 
    transformed_log_plots$MBP + ggtitle("Log-transformed data") +
    transformed_sct_plots$MBP + ggtitle("SCTransform") +
    transformed_tr_plots$MBP + ggtitle("Cell area normalization") +
    plot_annotation(title = "MBP") +
    patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect", nrow=2, heights = c(12,12)) & theme(legend.position = "none")
```

#### CX3CR1

```{r}
raw_plots$CX3CR1 + ggtitle("Raw data") + 
    transformed_log_plots$CX3CR1 + ggtitle("Log-transformed data") +
    transformed_sct_plots$CX3CR1 + ggtitle("SCTransform") +
    transformed_tr_plots$CX3CR1 + ggtitle("Cell area normalization") +
    patchwork::plot_annotation(title = "CX3CR1") +
    patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect", nrow=2, heights = c(12,12)) & theme(legend.position = "none")
```

#### FKBP5

```{r}
raw_plots$FKBP5 + ggtitle("Raw data") +

    transformed_sct_plots$FKBP5 + ggtitle("SCTransform") +
    transformed_tr_plots$FKBP5 + ggtitle("Cell area normalization") +
    plot_annotation(title = "FKBP5") +
```

#### PVALB

```{r}
raw_plots$PVALB + ggtitle("Raw data") +
    transformed_log_plots$PVALB + ggtitle("Log-transformed data") +
```
